contributions.headingText: McCune–Albright syndrome (MAS) is a sporadic disorder characterized by fibrous dysplasia of bone, café-au-lait skin lesions, and hyperfunctioning endocrinopathies.

Disease localization is probably determined by the developmental timing of the mutation, with earlier mutations resulting in more-widespread disease {3720010}. Fibrous dysplasia may affect any area of the skeleton. Skin lesions are typically located along the midline of the body but may extend to involve the limbs. Endocrinological disease typically involves the ovaries/testes, thyroid, pituitary, and/or adrenal glands. Involvement in any of these areas may occur in isolation or in combination with other disease features.

The clinical features of MAS are variable, depending on the distribution of mutation-bearing cells and the specific role of adenylyl cyclase and its second messenger cAMP in affected tissues. In general, most manifestations start during infancy and childhood {17501668; 22640971}. Fibrous dysplasia can be monostotic or polyostotic, and it presents with fractures, deformities, and pain {25719192}. Craniofacial fibrous dysplasia may uncommonly lead to neurological complications and functional deficits such as vision and hearing loss {17143235; 29192304; 29924878}. Hyperfunctioning endocrinopathies include precocious puberty (more common in females), hyperthyroidism, growth hormone excess, hyperprolactinaemia, and hypercortisolism {22640971}. Renal phosphate wasting due to excess FGF23 production by fibrous dysplasia cells may result in rickets/osteomalacia and bone pain {12952917}. Gastrointestinal features of MAS include pancreatic intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms {30124968}, gastric polyps {28188442}, and hepatobiliary lesions {24170100}. The association of fibrous dysplasia with intramuscular myxomas has previously been termed Mazabraud syndrome {30653046}; however, myxomas are more accurately denoted as an additional feature of MAS.

MAS is rare, and the prevalence has been estimated to be 1 case per 100 000 to 1 million people {25719192}. All racial and ethnic groups are affected equally. The prevalence is probably equal between males and females {25719192}.

The molecular basis for MAS is a postzygotic somatic mutation in exon 8 of GNAS that replaces the residue arginine at position 201 with histidine or cysteine {1944469; 15126527}. Pathogenic mutations occur at the p.Arg201 position in approximately 95% of patients, but infrequently other amino acid substitutions may occur {17493233; 10571700}. GNAS encodes the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G protein (Gsα), which couples heptahelical receptors for hormone and neurotransmitters to activate adenylyl cyclase. These mutations activate Gsα, which leads to constitutive activation of adenylyl cyclase and production of cAMP {1944469}.

In skin and endocrine tissues, Gsα activation leads to overproduction of hormones that signal through this receptor (MSH, LH, FSH, TRH, GHRH, and ACTH) {25719192}. In bone, Gsα activation leads to impaired differentiation and proliferation of skeletal stem cells {10365102}, resulting in formation of expansile bone lesions prone to fractures and deformity {25719192}.

Skeletal imaging shows typical non-aggressive expansile lesions, which may be present in one or multiple bones. Radiographically, lesions often have a homogeneous ground-glass appearance with cortical thinning {30484079}. Skin macules characteristically show jagged borders and a distribution respecting the midline of the body {22640971}. Ovarian cysts are intermittently visible on ultrasound and may appear simple or complex {27562402}. Testicular abnormalities can be detected by ultrasound in approximately 80% of boys, including focal hyperechoic and hypoechoic lesions and microlithiasis {22745241}. Thyroid abnormalities are visible on ultrasound in approximately two thirds of patients, even in the absence of frank hyperthyroidism, and include mixed cystic and solid lesions {18349068}. Pituitary involvement may show a variable appearance on MRI, including diffuse pituitary enlargement, macroadenoma, microadenoma, or normal findings {24517150; 22564667}.

Fibrous dysplasia lesions are composed of proliferating fibroblast-like bone marrow stromal cells, which replace normal bone and marrow. Osteoid trabeculae are present throughout the lesions and are discontinuous and non-functional in their orientation {10365102}. Trabeculae are frequently composed of poorly mineralized woven bone {10365102}. Follicular cysts lined by granulosa cells are frequently identified in girls and women with ovarian involvement {16789624; 171361}. In the testes, large foci of Leydig cell hyperplasia that cannot be definitively distinguished from Leydig cell tumours are commonly found; however, malignancy is very uncommon {22745241}. Thyroid findings commonly include follicular adenomas with papillary growth {9226216}, and rare cases of thyroid carcinoma have been reported {12970318}. Adrenal disease is characterized by unilateral or bilateral nodular hyperplasia with areas of atrophic cortex {21836496}.

Individuals with MAS have a variable prognosis depending on disease location and severity. Endocrinopathies persist throughout childhood and adulthood, with the exception of FGF23-mediated hypophosphataemia, which may worsen during periods of rapid linear growth and ameliorate in adulthood {23532406}. Endocrinopathies can generally be managed medically {25719192}, and optimizing endocrinopathies may improve skeletal outcomes in patients with fibrous dysplasia {15005844; 29669167; 29924878}. GNAS mutations in MAS are weakly oncogenic, and affected tissues probably carry a small increased risk of malignant transformation. Fibrous dysplasia rarely undergoes sarcomatous transformation {8111708; 13775207}; the risk may be increased by radiotherapy and uncontrolled growth hormone excess {2754454}. Women with MAS are at increased risk for breast cancer {28856726}.
